newsitem.title: YEMEN: Yemen reports high turnout for elections.
newsitem.headline: Yemen reports high turnout for elections.

text.p: Yemen reported a high turnout by voters in its first parliamentary elections since a 1994 civil war, but a soldier overshadowed Sunday's polling by killing eight people in an unexplained shooting.
"There was a very big turnout of around 80 percent," Saeed-al-Hekaimi, spokesman for the Supreme Election Committee, told a news conference in the capital Sanaa.

Before voting began, a soldier unexpectedly started shooting at people at a polling station in the town of Mukayras, killing five soldiers and three civilians, Interior Minister Hussein Mohammad Arab said.

"Seven people were immediately killed and two were injured when Abdullah Ahmed al-Barkani, a soldier on night duty, suddenly opened fire indiscriminately," he told a news conference. "One of the injured died later."
He said the soldier had been arrested and was being interrogated but there appeared to be no political motive for the killings.
But he added: "We were expecting more incidents because some people are discontented with holding general elections in Yemen." He did not elaborate.
Arab said one of the victims of the dawn attack was a member of Yemen's ruling party, the General Peoples Congress (GPC).

It was the third fatal assault in the run-up to the poll. A man was killed when clashes broke out between supporters of the GPC and its junior coalition partner, the Islamiost Islah Party, in Ibb on April 20 and a child was killed in Taiz on Thursday when gunmen opened fire at a GPC rally.
Hekaimi played down the violence, saying the attacks were "slight" and could have happened during elections anywhere in the world.

The Republic of Yemen, formed in 1990 by the merger of conservative North Yemen and Marxist South Yemen, had not held parliamentary elections since a seccessionist campaign by the south almost broke the country apart again in 1994.

The main opposition Yemen Socialist Party, some of whose former leaders launched the separatist campaign that sparked civil war, and three others boycotted the polls due to alleged irregularities. The government denied their charges.

Diplomats predicted that that President Ali Abdullah Saleh's GPC and Islah would retain power. Results were expected to start trickling in on Monday afternoon, but the final outcome was not likely to be known until later in the week.
A total of 2,306 candidates, including 17 women, stood for the 301 parliamentary seats, either under the banner of 12 parties or as independents.

Diplomats said the government hoped to boost its democratic image and provide the political stability needed to attract foreign investment and aid to the impoverished Arab state, a small oil producer.

They said they were encouraged by Yemen's democratic experiment but they noted that power ultimately rested with the president, his appointed ministers and military and security forces loyal to the GPC.
